First Light

The thing about January

2026 · 01 · 24  ·  9 min read

The thing about January, in this part of the country, is that the light comes in at an angle the rest of the year forgets. By eight in the morning the sun is already over the ridge but it is still pale, the color of a thing that has not warmed up yet, and it lies across the snow in long stripes that follow the shadows of the piñons. You can stand outside in your coat with a coffee mug and feel, for a moment, that the day has begun without you. Then a raven calls from somewhere down the arroyo and the spell loosens and you remember the woodbox is half empty and you have to drive into Española before noon.

I have been trying for years, without much success, to write down what January is actually like. Every year I think I will get it this time and every year I come up short. The trouble is that January resists summary in the same way a long marriage resists summary. There is too much that is true at once. It is the deadest month and also the most alert. It is when nothing happens and also when the year, secretly, decides what it is going to be. People say winter is quiet but anyone who has spent a January north of the thirty-fifth parallel knows that winter is loud — the wind in the stove pipe, the cracks in the beams when the temperature drops past zero, the snow sliding off the metal roof at three in the afternoon with a sound like a wet sigh.

What I notice most, though, is the way January changes the size of things. In summer the property feels small. The cottonwoods are full, the corrals are crowded with green, the irrigation ditch runs and the world seems to lean in close. In January everything stands back. The trees are thin and you can see between them all the way to the neighbor's barn, which is half a mile off. The light, which has nothing to bounce off of, just keeps going. You start to understand what people meant by sky in old books.

I do most of my shop work in the colder months, which surprises people when I say it. They imagine a carpenter working outdoors in summer, sun on his back, sawdust flying. But summer is for the land — the ditch, the garden, the fences that go down in monsoon season, the truck that needs the brakes done before the trip to Taos. Winter is when I can stand in the shop for nine hours and not feel guilty about it. The shop is unheated except for a small Jøtul in the corner that I light at six and bank at noon and refresh at three. By dusk the room is warm enough that I can work in a wool shirt, but the floor stays cold, and if I set a chisel down on the bench at the end of the day and pick it up the next morning, the steel is so cold it stings my palm. There is something honest about a tool that hurts a little when you greet it. It reminds you that the work is real.

A kiln, when you turn it off in winter, takes a long time to cool. I have a small electric one — nothing fancy, a hobbyist's kiln from the eighties that I bought used for two hundred dollars and rewired one weekend in 2021. I don't fire often. Maybe three times a year, and only small things: a bowl, a few mugs, once a set of tiles for the bathroom that turned out crookeder than I'd hoped but which my wife says she likes better that way. When I fire in January I leave the kiln in the shop overnight, and in the morning the room smells different. Not bad — clean, almost mineral, like a hot stone in a dry creek bed. The kiln itself is barely warm to the touch by then, but it has put its breath into the room and the room remembers. I think about that smell more than I should. It is one of the things I would miss if I had to leave here.

There is a particular task in January that I have come to look forward to in a way that I would not have predicted ten years ago, when I was still living in San Francisco and my idea of winter was a damp walk to the BART. The task is sweeping snow off a stack of green lumber. I keep a stack of pine — mostly ponderosa, some white fir — out behind the shop, on stickers, under a tin roof that does not quite reach far enough. So when the wind comes from the northwest, which it does in January, snow blows in sideways and settles on the top of the stack in a long thin drift. If you leave it there it melts in patches and the water finds its way down between the boards and you end up with a stack that dries unevenly, which is to say, a stack that warps. So once or twice a week, after a storm, I take a soft broom out and sweep.

It is not a hard job. It takes maybe twenty minutes. The broom makes a sound against the snow that is somewhere between a brush and a whisper, and the snow comes off the boards in little waves and falls down the side of the stack and disappears. When I am done the wood is dark and damp on top but it is exposed to the wind and the wind will dry it. I always stand there for a minute afterward and look at the stack and at the ridge beyond it. I am not thinking anything in particular. I am just standing there. This is, I think, the part of country life that the city does not understand and cannot be told. There is a great deal of standing.

I used to feel guilty about the standing. For the first year or two after we moved here I had this background hum of urgency — a residue, I think, from a decade in tech, where the worst thing you can be is idle. I would catch myself standing by the woodpile and think: I should be doing something. I should be billing. I should be answering an email. I should be writing the essay I owe by the end of the month. But over time the standing became a kind of work too. It is when I notice things. It is when I figure out what to do next. The shop runs better, I have come to believe, on the standing than on the sawing.

January is the month when the standing is hardest and most necessary. Hardest because it is cold and because the days are short and you feel that any minute not spent producing is a minute lost to the slow shrinking of the light. Necessary because there is nothing else to do. The garden is asleep. The ditch is dry. The truck is parked. Whatever is in the shop is in the shop and will get done when it gets done. You cannot rush a glue-up in a fifty-degree room. You cannot rush a finish in low humidity. You cannot rush the kiln. So you stand, and you sweep, and you wait, and slowly the year that is coming begins to take a shape you didn't know it was going to take.

I think about urgency a lot in January, which is funny because January is the month of the least objective urgency. There is no deadline outdoors. The deer come down through the orchard at dusk and they have nowhere to be either. And yet — I will be honest — there is a panic that comes around the second or third week of the month, every year, when the holidays are gone and the bills come and the day is over by five and I think: the year is already old. I am already behind. I should have done more last year and I am not doing enough now. It is a stupid feeling and I know it is a stupid feeling and I have it anyway. I think most people who do solitary work have some version of it. The remedy, for me, is the broom and the stack. You cannot panic productively while sweeping snow.

The smell of a wood stove before the door opens — this is a small thing but it is one of the great pleasures of the month, and I want to put it down before I lose it. You come in from outside, from sweeping or from feeding the dog or from chopping kindling, and the room is warm in that particular wood-warm way, and the stove is making its low metallic sound, and you walk over to it and put your hand on the door handle. There is a second, before you open it, when you can smell the fire through the seam. Not smoke — the stove is tight, there is no smoke — but the warm dry breath of the burning wood, faintly resinous, faintly sweet, like a room you used to know. Then you open the door and the heat hits your face and you put another piece on, and you close the door, and the room is the same room as before, but you have done something. The day is not entirely abstract.

Years ago a friend of mine, who is now dead, told me that the trick to winter was to stop thinking of it as a thing to get through. He said it like he was passing me a recipe. "Don't get through it," he said. "Be in it." At the time I was twenty-six and I thought he was being mystical and I rolled my eyes politely. Now I am older than he was when he said it, and I think he was just being accurate. Getting through January is a way of not being alive for a month. Being in it is harder because there is less to be in. The light is less. The sound is less. The company is less. But the less is the point. You have to learn to take the smaller portion and find it sufficient. Some years I manage this and some years I do not.

This year I am managing it, mostly. I have a chest of drawers on the bench that I have been building for a client in Santa Fe, walnut with poplar drawer sides, traditional dovetails because she asked, and the work is slow and good. I have been reading in the evenings — a long book about the history of the Rio Grande, which I keep falling asleep in, and a thinner book by a Japanese carpenter that I read three pages of at a time. The kiln is off until February. The stack out back is sweeped. The dog is asleep by the stove. Outside it is starting to snow again, very lightly, and the light is going from pale gold to pale blue to the color of nothing at all, and I am at the kitchen table writing this with a cup of tea that has gone cold an hour ago, and I am thinking, this is January, this is what it is, and there is nothing wrong with it.

What I would like to remember, when I read this back next year and the year after, is that the month was not a problem to be solved. The light came in at its angle. The kiln cooled overnight. The snow came off the lumber under the broom. The stove ticked through the morning. And whatever I needed to know about the year — which was not much, as it turned out — I learned by standing still.

Written at the kitchen table, Río Arriba County, New Mexico, late January 2026.
